To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

male rats search for food in a cuecontrolled spatial environment using a geometric representation of the environment which includes information about the identity and relative geometry of discrete landmark cues in the surrounding spatial field.
the identity of the landmarks and their geometric configuration are important for the spatial navigation of male rats.
landmark geometry and identity are both important for spatial navigation in rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how rats use landmark information to solve a new spatial problem, and how this information is represented in their spatial memory.
the nature and development of spatial representation in the rat.
the nature of the cognitive processes involved in spatial learning and memory, and with the role of the environment as an external memory aid in spatial learning and problem solving.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the landmark geometry and identity controls the spatial navigation of male rats.
landmark geometry is important to the spatial navigation and search performance of rats.
the rats in Experiment 1 used geometric representations of the landmarks to go to the bait locations, and that the landmarks in Experiments 2 & 3 were used for this purpose.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
landmark geometry and identity controls the spatial navigation in rats.
rats can use landmark geometry and identity to control spatial navigation.
rats use a geometric representation of the spatial environment that includes both the relative geometry of landmarks and their identity to navigate to a goal location.
The main takeaway from our work is that
rats are able to use the geometry of the environment, including both the identity and relative location of landmarks, to solve a spatial navigation problem.
the geometric properties of a spatial environment can have a profound effect on the ability of animals to navigate and search in it.
geometric representations of space are flexible enough to accommodate the presence of landmarks and that the presence of such landmarks can be used to enhance spatial search performance.
